items.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
items.content:
In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.

As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.

“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”

PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.

“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University .

“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University

Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.

Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”

To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”

AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security

After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.

“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”

items.title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
items.summary: networking
items.content:
It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working.

I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address.

I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address.

Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up .

But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one.

So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way.

For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver.

Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic.

But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit.

It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption.

You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses.

And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , only 7.03% of graded domains have a valid, fully validating DNSSEC chain.

If a tampered response fails DNSSEC validation, your resolver will return SERVFAIL instead of handing you that bogus IP address.

And yes, this is true. DoT and DoH rely on you trusting the DNS resolver you're sending your queries to. They encrypt the connection, so your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS traffic in transit. But that doesn't mean the resolver itself can't mess with your responses. You're still putting your trust in whoever runs that DNS server.

Indeed. Although your regular internet traffic is encrypted with TLS, your ISP can see the hostname during the TLS handshake (SNI). They can also figure out which site you're visiting just from the destination IP sometimes.

Unless, of course, you tunnel your traffic through a VPN. I use Mullvad through Tailscale's exit node feature.

Of course, this just shifts some of the trust to your VPN provider. But that's a story for another day.

items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.content:
I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games .

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play .

Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did .

In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.

I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here’s the chat transcript that built it.

It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-123036 📢 Source: redhat 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False A flaw was found in ansible-core. When a task marked `no_log: true` fails, the task result is censored before being emitted, but the `exception` field is retained because it is present in the PRESERVE allow-list in lib/ansible/_internal/_task.py, and the default stdout callback prints it through CallbackBase._handle_exception. As a result, sensitive values the operator explicitly asked to hide can be disclosed: module argument-validation errors echo the argument value, templating errors print an Origin source snippet (the failing line plus the two preceding lines of the variables file, exposing neighbouring secrets from an -e @secrets.yml file), and fail/assert messages are printed in full. Secret material supplied as extra variables or variables files can therefore leak to terminal output, CI logs, and the stdout logs of any automation wrapping ansible-playbook, even though every task touching the secrets is marked no_log: true. This is a regression introduced with the ansible-core 2.19 data-tagging/templating rework; the behaviour does not occur on 2.16, where the error text is correctly censored. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T09:38:31.304Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-123036

items.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
items.content:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

Confirmed residential proxy activity observed from the White House network, October 5 to November 3, 2026. What we observed

Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times .

Those exits came from 6 addresses , on 26 of the 30 days .

28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Pitcairn : 1 Starlink address, 1 observation.

Norfolk Island : 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations.

Svalbard : 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations.

Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7).

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

For relevant agencies: We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page .

items.title: Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower
items.summary: performance, rust, zig
items.content:
Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky – whose writings had a big influence my career – wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics . The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects.

One of his examples is the “Shlemiel the Painter” trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint.

It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs 1 , including now in 2026.

My Chess Analysis Service Staggers Under Load

A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online ↗ 2 . This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite.

While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds.

Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data – maybe about 40,000 records – into the data store took minutes . During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem.

What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time?

Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zig’s cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions.

A Minor Issue In Zig Becomes A Major Performance Issue

The project isn’t built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment – sqlite is of course a C project – so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild.

From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zig’s elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality.

Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time.

And that’s where the performance issue was introduced.

In the rewrite of strspn , replacing the musl version with the pure zig variant ), the first step measures the entire length of the string. This is also seen in the rewrites of strcspn, strpbrk and strstr.

This is a problem for tokenizers. A tokenizer takes a giant string and a common iterating step is to skip whitespace, getting the new string location and then repeating this pattern repeatedly. With this shlemiel the painter pattern introduced with these rewrites, as it steps through the text it is tokenizing it is remeasuring the entire length of the string endlessly.

This is what caused my performance issue, and it’s why it appeared on Linux but was never seen on my Mac (where zig wasn’t used for compiling sqlite).

Tokenizing a 1.2MB file, which was seen passing json to sqlite, is approximately 12,000x slower with this pattern. As the file gets larger, the slowdown is quadratic.

I mean no malice or disrespect to anyone involved with these great tools that enable so much. But it’s interesting that in the year 2026, these same old issues can recur, and…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
items.content:
Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.

In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.

Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg , Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.

Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.

“She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” Johnson’s note said. “The question now is how long the pause lasts.” As PIMCO head of public policy Libby Cantrill similarly warned, “even if statewide moratoria do not result, we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless—with more time required to secure permits and other approvals, as well as more concessions that data center developers will have to make.”

Texas wasn’t the only big shake-up. Democrats won governor races in the next three biggest states previously wooing data center developers—Arizona, Georgia, and Ohio. Overall, Axios projected that “nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity” could face similar delays as Hinojosa threatens in Texas. Bloomberg estimated that half the data centers in the US are now more vulnerable to scrutiny.

For AI firms, that’s a nightmare, since any delays will set back revenue, and IT consulting firm Gartner recently estimated “the AI boom is nearly $5 trillion short of paying for itself.”

Likely soon, developers nationwide will face tighter rules limiting tax incentives and requiring stronger protections for residents around who pays for grid infrastructure and water use. Those kinds of regulations will most likely increase developers’ costs at an inconvenient time, Bloomberg’s report said.

While many reports suggested that the first so-called “AI election” proved the power of the people to rein in Big Tech, some AI industry insiders downplayed the election results on Wednesday. items.title: PSA - Postman desktop modifies your coding agents to route API data via their own infrastructure
items.content:
Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.

What if making a diagram draggable was as simple as specifying what it can become?

Drag-and-drop makes the digital graspable. But designing bespoke drag interactions involves a lot of fiddly code to

handle geometry, feedback, and animations. As a result, many people, from educators to game designers,

mathematicians to creative tool builders, often don't bother.

worlds they inhabit, while helping them turn the rules of their worlds into rich tactile interactions in ours.

items.summary_ko: 다이어그램을 드래그 가능하게 만드는 일을, 그 요소가 될 수 있는 상태를 지정하는 것만큼 간단하게 만들자는 제안이다. 개발자가 요소별로 드래그 뒤에 도달해야 할 미래 상태를 지정하면, 시스템이 그 상태들을 미리 렌더링해 가능한 결과를 파악하고 이를 합쳐 부드러운 드래그 앤 드롭을 구현한다. 프로젝트는 사람들이 익숙한 의미 체계 안에서 계속 작업하면서 그 규칙을 촉각적 인터랙션으로 바꿀 수 있게 하는 것을 목표로 한다.

D2는 모델 기반(model-driven) 방식으로, 인터페이스 작성자가 드래그를 통해 접근 가능해야 할 모델 상태를 지정하면 엔진이 이 상태들을 미리 렌더링한다. 이후 본문은 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Kagi Blog - Education Shouldn't Be Held for Ransom
items.content:
If you ask any educator what the key to learning is, they won't say it's finding the right answer. They'll say it's what you gain from the struggle of getting there. Learning is found in the time and effort spent trying to understand an idea before it just "clicks."

That's what makes Google's latest announcement so galling to educators. Google announced this week that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for K-12 Google Workspace for Education accounts.

On the surface it sounds like a win for schools until you read the fine print: Google Search will be switched off along with them. Google's explanation, from Chris Phillips, its vice president for education, speaking to The New York Times , is that "Search and AI are deeply integrated," so one cannot be switched off without the other.

After the backlash, Google walked part of it back, saying schools could switch on Search by itself , without the rest of its Gemini products. But the core problem remains. Search still can't be used without AI features like AI Overviews.

The educators asking for choice aren't anti-technology. They have spent years in the classroom, and they know firsthand that handing kids AI-generated answers doesn't build critical thinking; it weakens it.

Search is how students reach the open web. A search engine that arrives only with AI attached isn't offering a choice. It's holding education for ransom.

A search engine is really an engine of discovery. When we search, we reflect, weigh, question, and synthesize, all at once. We’re exposed to rival sources and clashing perspectives, and we need sharp critical-thinking skills to discern the quality and relevance of what we find.

Technology companies are optimizing for speed. They talk about "removing friction," which is fine for unimportant things. There’s no benefit to friction when ordering takeout or getting a ride to the airport. But the same doesn't hold for education, because effort is the education. Friction, struggle, and perseverance is the learning. You simply can't speed-run understanding.

It helps to compare classroom learning with other kinds of training.

Imagine runners on the track team riding golf carts around the oval during "training" because the carts are faster and easier than running. They wouldn’t be preparing themselves to succeed in competition. That’s not how athletic training works. Progress is built out of sweat and discomfort.

Imagine band practice consisting of nothing but listening to Spotify, with no one painstakingly struggling to master their instruments or sheet music.

Science, math, and history are no different from athletics and music.

The best teachers rarely answer questions directly. They answer a question with a question of their own. The point isn't to hand over the answer but to make students wrestle with the question until they work it out on their own.

Likewise, a librarian doesn't hand you answers. A librarian's goal is to help you sharpen your research question and steer you toward better sources. That's the kind of help students need right now, especially in a world where the internet is being flooded by low quality AI slop. What students need more than ever are tools that teach them how to think, not what to think.

Information literacy is a practice, not a lesson

The educators I talk to aren't asking for a “magic wand.” They're asking for common-sense safeguards and controls that protect students at every grade level. This is scaffolding to make learning appropriate for all learners.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with giving students an AI answer occasionally, depending on the situation. But over-reliance can quickly turn into outsourcing the very thinking they’re in school to learn. The result over time is the acceptance without challenge of any information presented by AI. This is especially problematic when AI "hallucinates" or fabricates information.

Educators should get to decide when and how AI shows up for…

items.title: Your Cryptography Conspiracy Theory Is Wrong
items.summary: cryptography
items.content:
This conversation plays out hundreds of times a day, but (thankfully) only a handful of those involve me:

Cryptography nerd: “Oh, you probably want to use [sensible recommendation].”

Person: “Ah, well, can I really trust that? The NSA probably backdoored it 30 years ago. Dual_EC, amirite?!”

Koblitz and Menezes, unheard: “ You fucking wot m8? “

Conspiracy theories about the NSA and/or NIST are a dime a dozen these days. And, ever since the Snowden disclosures in 2013, I am politically primed to directionally agree with distrusting the US government wholesale.

But most of the technical arguments baked into folks’ conspiracy theories make no goddamn sense .

This distrust is not exclusive to only the US government.

The goal of this blog post is not to convince you that you should trust any government; just that they are not magical or omniscient.

To that end, I’m going to explore some of the history of NSA, NIST, and cryptography standardization. Then, to explore some of the conspiracy theories that were being floated about such activity, and what we’ve learned in the years since (especially in the past month). Finally, I’m going to examine some of the current conspiracy theories floating around message boards and social media today, and explain why they’re almost certainly wrong.

Buckle up, this is going to be a tedious one.

If you find yourself asking a question like this, the correct answer is simply, “You shouldn’t.”

After all, I have never held (let alone even applied for) a security clearance, and have no access to any non-public information. I’m also not a current or former government employee, and have no aspirations to ever become one. I have access to all the same facts anyone else does.

In balance, I have no horse in the race of who trusts whom. I’m just tired of hearing the same poorly reasoned arguments all the damn time, and would like to stop having to repeat myself when I encounter one.

The sources for this, by the way, are the declassified United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and United States Cryptologic History .

The Data Encryption Standard (DES) was published in the Federal Register in 1975 and then standardized in 1977.

We consider it weak these days, but DES was a real game-changer for its time: It offered a standard block cipher to use for sensitive (but not classified) commercial applications. Prior to DES, the history of cryptography was largely about military uses (except a few quirky mathematicians here and there), going back before Caesar’s cipher .

From declassified documents, we now know the full story, but from the time that DES was first standardized, up until recent years, there have been a concerns about NSA’s involvement .

We sent the S-boxes off to Washington. They came back and were all different.

Alan Konheim, quoted in Applied Cryptography , p. 280

To say that academics did not trust DES would be putting it mildly: Martin Hellman (who, with Whitfield Diffie and Ralph Merkle, invented public-key cryptography) sent a letter in 1975 to the National Bureau of Standards that stated:

Whit Diffie and I have become concerned that the proposed data encryption standard, while probably secure against commercial assault, may be extremely vulnerable to attack by an intelligence organization.

Martin Hellman, re-published in this paper in 1990.

At the heart of the concern about DES was something called an S-box, which simply maps an input to an output, but whose purpose is to provide a non-linear transformation to obscure the relationship between the ciphertext and the key.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: After Texas’ blue wave, what happens to Elon Musk and SpaceX? “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
items.content:
Following his public disputes with California authorities during the COVID-19 pandemic, Elon Musk personally moved to Texas, outside of Austin, in 2020.

Over the next six years, he doubled down on the Lone Star State. In 2021, Musk increasingly focused the Starship program in South Texas, urging SpaceX employees to move there and work on the company’s future. In March of that year, he began using the name Starbase to describe the production and launch facilities near the Rio Grande River.

In 2023, he built a massive factory east of Austin to manufacture customer terminals and other electronics for the Starlink program. In July 2024, he announced that SpaceX would relocate its corporate headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas. He cited California’s regulatory and political environment as the motivating factor.

Since then, Musk has continued with major expansions of the Starbase facility. This summer, his company announced that Terafab, “the most epic-chip building effort in the world,” would be built in Grimes County, Texas, and that “a vertically integrated factory with more than 100 million square feet of manufacturing space is planned,” the company said . That’s right, 100 million square feet. This is equivalent to 1,700 American football fields, 15 Pentagons, or three Central Parks.

Everything is bigger in Texas, of course, and for a time, so was the bromance between Musk and Texas politicians. He has repeatedly said he loves Texas’ political climate, its regulatory environment, and the state’s Republican leaders. And in turn, they have loved him back. In July , Texas Gov. Greg Abbott praised Musk before interviewing him as a guest host of The Sean Hannity Show as “the leading visionary of our time. Thomas Edison. Just like that, maybe even bigger.”

During the 2026 midterms, Musk went all in on Republicans, investing nearly half a billion dollars in their election campaigns through his own America PAC and other organizations, according to The New York Times. Of this estimated $474 million, nearly half went to candidates in Texas.

And then, on Tuesday, a historic blue wave washed over the formerly deep-red state. Most of Musk’s political friends in Texas will soon be gone. So what happens next?

We don’t really know. But there are some important things to watch.

First up is Musk’s public comments on the social media site he owns, X. Throughout the evening on Tuesday, as it became clear Republicans were headed for a historic defeat, Musk remained uncharacteristically quiet. His first comment came 12 minutes after midnight in Texas, where the key statewide races had all been called.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote . A bit later, he tried to react with some sarcastic humor and then largely went back to promoting SpaceX’s AI Grok bot and the Starlink Internet service.

I think we can read a lot into this, drawing on my own understanding of Musk’s motivations and conversations with a couple of people familiar with his thinking.

Politically, Musk has changed his stripes before. He bundled for President Obama’s campaigns and endorsed Hillary Clinton for president in 2016. Later, of course, he took a hard-right turn, becoming Donald Trump’s most prominent and largest financial backer in the 2024 presidential campaign.

Now there are two avenues open to Musk. He can lean further into Republicans and far-right politics. He still has allies there and could look to become a kingmaker in selecting the party’s 2028 presidential nominee. He could also expand his footprint in other red states (more on this below).

The alternative, which would be consistent with some of his past behavior, is for Musk to moderate politically. But are Democrats interested in de-escalation after such a decisive victory? Welcome to another issue of Haskell Weekly!

Haskell is a safe, purely functional programming language with a fast, concurrent runtime.

This is a weekly summary of what’s going on in its community.

A Specialised Haskell Processor on FPGA by Yukang Xie

I follow Lennart Augustsson’s approach when he was presenting MicroHs — give the demo first. This is a Haskell program running on a specialised processor, which is hosted on an FPGA and talks through a UART port.

An LC-3 Disassembler in Haskell by Abhinav Sarkar

LC-3 assembly is an educational programming language. It is simple enough that complex programs can be written directly in it without needing a compiler, and thus it is often used in teaching assembly. An LC-3 textual assembly program is compiled to a binary object file by an assembler, and then executed by a virtual machine. Writing a virtual machine for LC-3 is a fun little exercise. However, in this post, we implement a disassembler for compiled LC-3 binaries back to textual assembly programs.

Building a DJ set is finding a path on a graph (and how this became a Haskell program) by Daniele Filaretti

Long story short, I ended up building a small Haskell program to help me plan DJ sets. This post explains where the idea came from and how the problem can be described simply using graphs. It also gives an overview of how the source code is organized and how its main parts relate to the theoretical concepts discussed here. The full code is available on GitHub.

Episode 88 – Tom Schrijvers by The Haskell Interlude

In this Haskell Interlude, we sat down with Tom Schrijvers, the head of the Functional Programming team at KU Leuven. He has been a prolific contributor to the foundations of Haskell, with many papers pushing the boundaries of the Haskell type system, programming with effects, and applications of functional programming.Our conversation was a whirlwind tour through Tom’s long and wide publication history, with lots of tangents and ideas about functional programming, logic programming, constraints, DSLs, composition, program calculation, and other great stuff.

Haskell Foundation monthly updates; October by The Haskell Foundation

The Haskell Foundation is making an effort to communicate more often. It’s time to resurrect the monthly updates. We’re aiming to have an update for the first Monday of every month.

Hypha: navigating Haskell source code for humans and machines by Alfredo Di Napoli

TL;DR I’m releasing a beta version of Hypha, an experimental CLI tool for Haskell development which can be useful to explore your project dependencies, read documentation offline without the need of generating Haddock files, and use LLM harnesses and tools without hammering Hackage or Hoogle. Think of Hypha as an offline-first, enhanced version of your Cabal store.

Musical Signal Functions by Sandy Maguire

We’ve been chatting for a few days about my vision for a constructive model of music. So far it’s been rather loosey-goosey; lots of vibes, some semantics, but nothing in the way of implementation. Today let’s get our boots muddy and do enough implementation that we have something concrete to talk about.

Now supporting the newer and released brillo 3.0.0, with some minor changes to the code.

Since it is popular to have an AI policy these days, here is the one for the MicroHs project.

items.summary_ko: FPGA에서 동작하는 Haskell 전용 프로세서가 UART 포트로 통신하는 데모와, LC-3 바이너리를 텍스트 어셈블리로 되돌리는 Haskell 디스어셈블러 구현 글을 소개한다. DJ 세트를 구성하는 일을 그래프 위의 경로 찾기로 보는 글도 포함되어 있다. 이 뉴스레터는 매주 Haskell 커뮤니티의 소식을 요약한다.
items.content_ko: Haskell 커뮤니티의 주간 소식을 모은 뉴스레터 549호다. Yukang Xie의 A Specialised Haskell Processor on FPGA는 FPGA에 올린 전용 프로세서에서 Haskell 프로그램이 실행되고 UART 포트로 통신하는 모습을 먼저 보여준다. LC-3는 컴파일러 없이도 복잡한 프로그램을 직접 쓸 만큼 단순해 어셈블리 교육에 자주 쓰인다. 원문에는 DJ 세트를 만드는 과정을 그래프 위의 경로 찾기로 보는 글도 소개되어 있으나, 본문이 끊겨 세부 내용은 확인할 수 없다.

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: go
items.content:
Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs.

Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0.

We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.

Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!

This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages.

Overall, encoding/json has held up well.

The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types

with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to

customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.

However, in the years since its introduction,

various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json :

Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen

increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate.

Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs,

to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different

(successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,

whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.

The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,

instead of introducing silent data corruption,

encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.

RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,

so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,

merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.

The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value

without a universally agreed upon meaning.

This could be exploited by attackers in security applications

and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ).

The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with

programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled

into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.

Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null ,

this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.

indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps

are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

Case-insensitive unmarshaling : When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name

is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match.

This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

Inconsistent calling of methods : Due to an implementation detail,

MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver

are inconsistently called by encoding/json . While regarded as a bug,

this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:

It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader .

Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v) ,

which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types,

but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions.

Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces

cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Ouch: The Raspberry Pi 5 just hit an eye-watering $385
items.content:
PCWorld reports that the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB model has surged from $120 to an eye-watering $385, with rising RAM costs driving the dramatic price hike.

The Pi Compute Module 5 has also seen price increases, and high demand is fueling scalping issues that make these boards even harder to find affordably.

The manufacturer suggests these price increases may be temporary, though no clear timeline for a return to normal pricing has been indicated.

The times, they are a-changin’, and not for the better. Raspberry Pi is the archetypal single-board project PC. Its monster popularity comes down to its open nature, easy-to-work-on layout, and its low price. But while data centers devour the world’s RAM supply , low prices are a thing of the past. The latest round of price increases makes the 16GB variant of the Raspberry Pi 5 a whopping $385 USD.

The slim Pi Compute Module 5 16GB also gets a price bump, from $335 to $375. According to CEO Ebon Upton , the company is trying to hold out on price increases for the Pi 500+ PC-in-a-keyboard , and I assume that’s possible just because they sell fewer of those than the regular Pi devices.

That brings the recent, full-power Pi lineup pricing to this grim table, going by today’s prices on PiShop US:

Just for a quick comparison, the Pi 5 launched in 2023 with the 4GB variant starting at $60 . The 16GB version debuted in January 2025 for just $120 . It’s now more than 300 percent as expensive, almost entirely due to memory price increases. The various models are also experiencing shortages, with the usual scalping problems tagging along.

Upton says that the latest price increases are driven by a lack of alternatives, but that the current landscape is “ultimately temporary.” “We look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again.” Here’s hoping.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-112072 📢 Source: Echo 💣 CVSS Score: 6.5 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True vault-java-driver, a Java client for HashiCorp Vault, parses Vault's JSON responses with a vendored minimal-json parser that has no nesting depth limit. A deeply nested value raises a StackOverflowError, which escapes catch (Exception) handlers and kills the reading thread. A Vault token that can write but not read a KV v2 path can store such a value there, so every later read of that path through the driver fails. This requires Vault 1.19.x or earlier, because 1.20 and later reject values nested deeper than 298 levels. This issue affects io.github.jopenlibs:vault-java-driver 5.2.0 through 6.2.3 and is fixed in 7.0.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T07:57:30.653Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112072
items.title_ko: [CVE-2026-112072] vault-java-driver, 중첩 깊이 제한 부재로 StackOverflowError 유발 가능
items.summary_ko: vault-java-driver의 내장 JSON 파서에는 중첩 깊이 제한이 없어, 깊게 중첩된 Vault 응답 값이 StackOverflowError를 일으키고 읽기 스레드를 종료시킬 수 있다. 쓰기만 가능한 토큰으로 이런 값을 KV v2 경로에 저장하면 이후 드라이버를 통한 읽기가 계속 실패할 수 있다. 영향 버전은 5.2.0~6.2.3이며 7.0.0에서 수정되었다(CVSS 6.5, MEDIUM).
items.content_ko: vault-java-driver는 HashiCorp Vault용 Java 클라이언트로, 내장된 minimal-json 파서가 중첩 깊이를 제한하지 않는다. 깊게 중첩된 값은 StackOverflowError를 일으켜 catch (Exception) 처리를 빠져나가 읽기 스레드를 종료시킬 수 있다. KV v2 경로에 쓰기만 가능한 Vault 토큰으로 그런 값을 저장하면, 이후 드라이버로 해당 경로를 읽을 때마다 실패할 수 있다. 이 문제는 Vault 1.19.x 이하에서만 해당하며, 1.20 이상은 298단계보다 깊게 중첩된 값을 거부한다. 영향 버전은 5.2.0~6.2.3이며 7.0.0에서 수정되었다. CVSS 6.5(MEDIUM), 원격 악용 가능으로 표시되어 있다. 공개일은 2026-11-05다.

items.title: Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode
items.summary: css, web
items.content:
by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

items.summary_ko: Safari 27.3 베타에 적응형 다크 모드가 추가되었다. 사용자가 이 기능을 켜면 Safari가 밝은 배경의 웹사이트를 어두운 화면으로 바꿔 보여준다. 다크 모드를 지원한다고 명시한 사이트는 기존 그대로 표시된다.
items.content_ko: Safari는 2019년 Safari 12.1에서 웹 다크 모드를 처음 지원했다. 현재 다크 모드 사용자는 웹 페이지 로드의 약 40%를 차지하지만, 다크 모드를 지원하는 페이지는 약 10%에 불과하다. 적응형 다크 모드는 이 격차를 줄이기 위한 기능으로, 웹 전반에서 일관된 어두운 화면을 제공하는 것이 목표다. 사용하려면 시스템 외관을 어둡게 설정한 뒤 밝은 배경의 웹사이트에 접속하면 된다. 그러면 Safari가 적응형 다크 모드 미리보기를 제안하며, ‘Try’를 누르면 적용된다. 웹사이트가 color-scheme 메타 태그나 CSS 속성으로 다크 모드 지원을 밝힌 경우에는 변경되지 않는다. 나머지 사이트는 색상 등을 분석해 적용 여부를 판단한다. 본문이 중간에 끊겨 있어 판단 기준의 세부 내용은 확인되지 않는다.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
items.content:
The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.

“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”

The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website , which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”

The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”

The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.

“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

When testing the Brave browser for Mac today, we found that the optional “paywall blocker” feature made it possible to read a paywalled New York Times article. The feature was enabled in the default settings and can be turned off.

The NYT asked for a permanent injunction to stop Brave from continuing the allegedly illegal conduct. The lawsuit seeks statutory damages, actual damages, restitution of profits derived from alleged copyright infringement, and “restitution and disgorgement of all revenue and profits Brave obtained through its ad-substitution scheme.”

A similar lawsuit was filed against Brave in the same court yesterday by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel companies. “AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” said Steven Lieberman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.”

We contacted Brave and will update this article if it provides a response. Perplexity, which is not a defendant in the Brave lawsuit but is facing a different lawsuit filed by the NYT, accused the news organization of “disinformation” in a statement provided to Ars and other news outlets. Perplexity’s statement did not identify any specific inaccuracies in the lawsuit against Brave.

items.title: 의뢰 맡깁니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-109408 📢 Source: Echo 💣 CVSS Score: 7.4 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True vault-java-driver, a Java client for HashiCorp Vault, silently disables TLS certificate and hostname verification in three states where the caller asked for verification: an SslConfig passed to VaultConfig without calling build(), an SslConfig restored by Java deserialization, and VAULT_SSL_VERIFY set to a truthy value other than "true", such as 1, yes or on. In each case SslConfig.isVerify() returns false and the driver installs a trust-all SSLContext. An attacker on the network path to the Vault server can then read the Vault token and secrets in transit and forge responses. This issue affects io.github.jopenlibs:vault-java-driver 5.2.0 through 6.2.3. It is fixed in 7.0.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T07:36:07.410Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109408
